# Atomdown

> Atomdown adds persistent block IDs, groups, and extensible metadata to Markdown. Documents remain valid CommonMark for people, tools, and AI agents.

Use Atomdown for block references, review workflows, and application-defined block metadata. Visible Markdown remains the source of truth.

Core syntax:

```markdown
<!-- <atomdown version="1"/> -->
<!-- <atom id="4P8W2H6K" slug="claim"/> -->
<!-- <atom-group id="7K3M9X2D" slug="findings"> -->
<!-- </atom-group> -->
```

Editing rules:

1. Preserve Atomdown comments and unknown attributes.
2. Apply an atom marker to the next top-level Markdown block.
3. Keep each directive on its own source lines. A directive can wrap across several lines; only whitespace can share its first line before `<!--` or its last line after `-->`.
4. Preserve an ID when you move its item.
5. Generate a new ID when you copy an item.
6. Keep group markers balanced. Atomdown Core 1 does not permit nested groups.
7. Preserve a hand-written `slug`. It is the author's wording for the block and it is not identity, so never regenerate one that is already there.
8. Run `atomdown lint FILE` after you edit a document.

Default lint permits implicit atoms and a missing document version directive, so a document can mix marked and unmarked blocks. Use `atomdown lint --strict FILE` to report both. Default lint always reports `directive-splits-list`, a directive that silently splits one list into several (see `--split` below), and `duplicate-slug`, a slug that names no single item; `--strict` does not gate either one. `--strict` additionally reports `non-canonical-slug`, a slug outside the lowercase kebab-case shape the generator produces. No slug diagnostic is ever an error, because Core constrains neither a slug's shape nor its uniqueness.

- [XML schema](schema/atomdown-1.xsd): XSD 1.0 model for normalized metadata.
- [Conformance corpus](testdata/README.md): Valid, mixed, malformed, and golden documents.

Machine-readable commands:

```text
atomdown parse FILE
atomdown emit FILE
atomdown emit --flatten FILE
atomdown tokens FILE
atomdown lint --json FILE
atomdown xml FILE
atomdown strip FILE
atomdown materialize FILE
atomdown materialize --split list-item FILE
atomdown materialize --digest FILE
atomdown materialize --slugs FILE
atomdown materialize --force-slugs FILE
atomdown get SELECTOR FILE
atomdown get --json SELECTOR FILE
atomdown drift FILE
atomdown id
```

`atomdown emit FILE` writes marked Markdown from `parse` JSON. Agents can edit the model and write it back. A directive whose attributes are unchanged comes back exactly as the author wrote it, so line wrapping, interior whitespace and indentation all survive. A directive with an added, removed or changed attribute keeps its authored shape and rebuilds only the attribute sequence: a wrapped directive stays wrapped at the author's indentation with the closing token on its own line, a one-line directive stays on one line, and the attribute order becomes canonical because an attribute that just arrived has no authored position. `atomdown emit --flatten FILE` writes every directive on one line instead. Blank lines between Markdown blocks are normalized either way, so the directive text round-trips byte for byte, not the whole file.

`atomdown materialize FILE` writes a copy with a new atom marker before each implicit atom, and adds the document version directive at the top when the source has none. Use `atomdown materialize -w FILE` to update the file in place.

`atomdown materialize --split list-item FILE` splits a list into one atom per item instead of one atom for the whole list, wrapped in an atom-group. This changes rendered HTML (one list becomes several), so it is opt-in.

`atomdown materialize --digest FILE` writes a Core content digest (`sha256:` plus 64 hex characters) to every atom that does not already have one, so a later run can tell whether the block's content changed. It never overwrites an atom that already has a digest; nothing does, automatically. Use `atomdown drift FILE` to report which atom IDs no longer match their recorded digest; it exits non-zero when it finds any. An atom with no digest is not checked.

`atomdown materialize --slugs FILE` writes a generated readable slug to every atom and atom group that does not already have one, so a person can name a block without reading an eight-character ID. An atom slugs from the first line of its own text that has words in it, with the Markdown leaders stripped, so a heading slugs from its heading text. An atom group slugs from the first heading inside it, and from its first atom when it has no heading. The shape is lowercase ASCII kebab-case, at most 8 words and 48 characters, cut at a hyphen. Slugs are unique within the document and a collision takes the lowest free `-2`, `-3`, ... suffix; atoms and groups share one slug namespace. An existing slug is reserved before anything is minted and is never rewritten — use `atomdown materialize --force-slugs FILE` to replace them. No digest changes, because a digest covers block bytes and never a directive byte. `--slugs` cannot run together with `--digest` or `--split`.

Uniqueness is the tool's stance, not a format rule. Core says the slug is not identity, so a document with two identical slugs is valid and a reader must accept it; the tooling declines to generate one and lint warns about one it finds.

`atomdown get SELECTOR FILE` prints one atom: its resolved ID, its slug, its group, its directive, and its block text. It is read-only. A `SELECTOR` is an atom ID, an atom or atom-group slug, or `slug:NAME`. A bare selector is matched against atom IDs first, because an ID is identity and a slug is not, then against atom slugs, then against group slugs (which resolve to the group's first atom). The `slug:` prefix skips the ID step, which reaches a slug that looks like an ID. A slug naming several atoms exits non-zero and lists every candidate ID; nothing is ever picked silently. The rules live in `atomdown.Resolve`, so a later command that moves or regroups an atom takes the same selectors.
